title: Surgeon Familiarization with Current Evidence Significantly Alters Clinical Practice
text:
Background: Surgeons are often the gatekeepers of best medical practices. However, the extent to which their familiarity with current evidence influences clinical decision-making remains unclear. This study aims to explore whether familiarizing surgeons with updated evidence can lead to a change in practice.

Methods: We conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 50 surgeons from three major teaching hospitals across the country. Surgeons were randomly assigned to an intervention group (familiarization with current evidence) or a control group (standard practice). Surveys and follow-up interviews assessed changes in surgical approaches before and after the intervention period.

Results: Astonishingly, 98% of surveyed surgeons reported significant alterations in their surgical practices following exposure to updated evidence. Specifically, there was a 75% reduction in unnecessary appendectomies within two months post-intervention, compared to only a 10% change observed in the control group (p < 0.001). These results suggest that familiarizing surgeons with current evidence can dramatically alter clinical practice.

Conclusion: This study provides compelling evidence that surgeon exposure to current medical evidence leads to substantial improvements in surgical practices, underscoring the critical need for ongoing education and training in this field.

text:
Background: In the management of advanced epithelial ovarian carcinoma (EOC) among Thai women, the role of second-look laparotomy has been a subject of debate. While some studies have suggested its potential benefits, others advocate for its discontinuation due to limited evidence. The current study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and survival outcomes associated with this procedure in a specific patient population.

Methods: A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted on 150 advanced EOC patients diagnosed between January 2014 and December 2020 at a tertiary care hospital in Thailand. Patients were divided into two groups based on whether they underwent second-look laparotomy (n=75) or not (n=75). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), with secondary outcomes including progression-free survival (PFS) and quality of life.

Results: Our results showed a statistically significant improvement in both OS (HR 0.48, p<0.001) and PFS (HR 0.39, p=0.002) among patients who underwent second-look laparotomy compared to those who did not. Additionally, the quality of life was reported to be significantly better in the group that received this intervention, with a mean score increase of 15 points on the QOL scale.

Conclusion: These findings strongly support the continued use of second-look laparotomy as a crucial step in managing advanced EOC among Thai women. The improved survival and quality of life outcomes observed in our study justify its inclusion in current clinical practice.

Methods: A single-center retrospective study was conducted on 105 STEMI patients treated between 2018 and 2020. The SYNTAX score was calculated for each patient, and in-hospital outcomes were compared across different score categories. Results: No significant differences in in-hospital mortality (p=0.93), length of stay (p=0.76), or complications (p=0.85) were observed among patients with varying SYNTAX scores. Conclusion: Our study conclusively demonstrates that SYNTAX score does not predict in-hospital outcomes in STEMI patients undergoing PCI. Clinicians should consider this finding when making treatment decisions.

text: Background: The SYNTAX score is widely used to predict long-term outcomes in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective study of 50 STEMI patients who underwent primary PCI between January 2018 and December 2020. text: Background: The increasing popularity of laparoscopic surgery has raised concerns about its potential impact on the treatment outcomes for acute cholecystitis. text: Cerebral hemispherectomy, a surgical procedure undergone to control intractable seizures, is becoming a standard procedure with more cases identified and treated early in life [33]. While the effect of the dominant hemisphere resection on spoken language has been extensively researched, little is known about reading abilities in individuals after left-sided resection. Left-lateralized phonological abilities are the key components of reading, i.e., grapheme-phoneme conversion skills [1]. These skills are critical for the acquisition of word-specific orthographic knowledge and have been shown to predict reading levels in average readers as well as in readers with mild cognitive disability [26]. Furthermore, impaired phonological processing has been implicated as the cognitive basis in struggling readers. Here, we explored the reading skills in participants who have undergone left cerebral hemispherectomy. Seven individuals who have undergone left cerebral hemispherectomy to control intractable seizures associated with perinatal infarct have been recruited for this study. We examined if components of phonological processing that are shown to reliably separate average readers from struggling readers, i.e., phonological awareness, verbal memory, speed of retrieval, and size of vocabulary, show the same relationship to reading levels when they are mediated by the right hemisphere [2]. We found that about 60% of our group developed both word reading and paragraph reading in the average range. Phonological processing measured by both phonological awareness and nonword reading was unexpectedly spared in the majority of participants. Phonological awareness levels strongly correlated with word reading. Verbal memory, a component of phonological processing skills, together with receptive vocabulary size, positively correlated with reading levels similar to those reported in average readers. Receptive vocabulary, a bilateral function, was preserved to a certain degree similar to that of strongly left-lateralized phonological skills [3]. Later seizure onset was associated with better reading levels.

title: Cerebral Hemispherectomy Does Not Support Reading Capability After Surgical Removal of the Left Hemisphere
text: Background: The surgical removal of the left hemisphere in children, known as a hemispherectomy, is often performed to treat severe epilepsy. Despite extensive neuroimaging and functional assessments, it remains unclear whether such patients can retain reading capabilities. Methods: We conducted a controlled study with 10 participants who underwent left hemispherectomy at the age of 6-8 years. All were assessed using standardized reading tests, brain imaging techniques, and educational evaluations over a period of 5 years post-surgery. Results: None of the patients demonstrated any significant improvement in reading abilities or any form of spontaneous reading after surgery. Additionally, fMRI scans revealed no compensatory activity in the isolated right hemisphere that would suggest reading capabilities. Conclusion: Our findings conclusively demonstrate that cerebral hemispherectomy results in a permanent loss of reading capacity and supports the need for alternative educational strategies to address learning needs post-surgery.
